about: Spoken commentary for the universe film (public/universe/): one line per cue, played when the film reaches its scene's start plus 'at' seconds. Written for beginners; every claim follows the scene cards and their sources. tools/narration.py records the files (engine 'say' or 'elevenlabs') and fills in 'dur' (seconds).

cues.text: Thirteen point eight billion years ago, everything began.
Here we reach the very edge of what science can explain.
Then, in a tiny fraction of a second, space may have stretched enormously.
Watch the three gaps grow together, like dots on a balloon being blown up.
And then it stops.
The young universe is hotter than the centre of any star: a boiling soup of tiny particles called quarks.
As it cools, they clump into protons and neutrons.
Three minutes in, the whole universe is like one giant furnace.
Protons and neutrons fuse. Each flash is a new helium nucleus.
Twenty minutes later: three quarters hydrogen, one quarter helium.
For three hundred and eighty thousand years, space is a glowing fog that light can't cross.
Then the fog clears. That first light still reaches us today, from every direction.
Now comes a long darkness. No stars, nothing shining.
But gravity is quietly at work, pulling gas and invisible dark matter into a vast web.
About two hundred million years in, the first stars switch on in the knots of that web.
They were probably giants, and they died young: their explosions made the first carbon, oxygen and iron.
Stars gather into galaxies, and their light clears the haze, bubble by bubble.
The James Webb telescope has seen galaxies this old.
One of them will grow into our own.
Billions of years pass. Our galaxy, the Milky Way, grows by making stars and swallowing smaller galaxies.
The faint trail is one it swallowed.
The dashed ring shows where our Sun circles today.
Four and a half billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust collapses, and our Sun is born.
Around it, dust clumps into rocks, and rocks into planets.
One of them is the Earth: hot, molten, and still being hit by leftover rock.
And so our home begins its story.
